outputs.L1:
Editor’s note: Carly Fiorina is chief executive of Carly Fiorina Enterprises and former chief executive of HP. She was an adviser to Sen. John McCain’s presidential campaign last year. Carly Fiorina says outrage at Wall Street pay is justified, but salaries should not be set by government.

(CNN) — Americans are outraged by excessive CEO pay and perks. That outrage is justified, particularly when American taxpayers are footing the bill.

Our capitalist system works best when there is transparency and accountability. There has been too little of both on Wall Street. Inevitably, the president and Congress are now attempting to respond to taxpayer anger and restore some “common sense,” as President Obama recently declared, to CEO compensation.

The proposed solution caps top executive pay at $500,000 for institutions that have received bailout money. I do not believe this is the answer, although it is an understandable reaction. It is arbitrary: Why not $400,000 or $600,000? It is incomplete: It applies only to institutions that will receive additional government assistance going forward. And it does not strengthen our economy when government decides how much each job is worth. In America, we leave that role to markets.

So what is the answer?

To strengthen transparency, all aspects of CEO pay and perks should be fully disclosed on a regular basis. This should include airplanes, cars, golf-club memberships, bonuses, stock options, retirement plans, and salaries—in short, everything that a common-sense person would consider part of a CEO reward package. See Fiorina discuss executive pay, including her own »

To strengthen accountability, all aspects of CEO compensation should be voted on by shareholders annually. Ultimately, it is the owners of a company who must determine whether a CEO’s rewards are justified by a CEO’s performance. And because the American taxpayer is now a partial owner of many companies, the government can get a vote as well—in some cases, a very sizeable vote.

In addition, “clawback provisions,” which require a CEO to return compensation to shareholders if promised results are not delivered, should be standard practice.

Finally, when a company comes to Washington for American taxpayer money, it is an admission that mistakes have been made and major bets have failed. These CEOs should be prepared to tender their resignations and those of their boards. To earn a bailout, a CEO and board should be held accountable.

We should not weaken our economy while trying to fix it.

These are difficult times. President Obama has described our current situation as a “crisis” and an impending “catastrophe.” In such times, action is required. The key is to take actions that help in the short term while also being sensible for the medium and long term.

Too often, our politicians react to crisis and public anger by overreaching, creating new and unforeseen problems that become clear only with the passage of time.

In this country, the opportunity to be rewarded for taking prudent risks is fundamental to our economic vitality and strength. Let us not lose that fundamental principle in our outrage over Wall Street greed and excess.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Carly Fiorina.
outputs.L2:
Editor’s note: Carly Fiorina is the CEO of Carly Fiorina Enterprises and previously served as chief executive of HP. She advised Sen. John McCain’s presidential campaign the previous year. Fiorina argues that anger over Wall Street compensation is warranted, but that the government should not determine salaries.

(CNN) — Many Americans are furious about outsized pay packages and benefits for chief executives. Their anger is understandable, especially when taxpayers are paying the cost. Capitalism functions most effectively when openness and responsibility are present, and Wall Street has shown too little of either.

As a result, the president and Congress are trying to answer public frustration and bring what President Obama recently called “common sense” back to executive compensation. Their proposal would limit the pay of top executives to $500,000 at companies that have received bailout funds.

While that response is understandable, I do not believe it is the right solution. The number is arbitrary: Why $500,000 rather than $400,000 or $600,000? It is also limited, since it applies only to institutions receiving additional government help in the future. More importantly, our economy is not strengthened when government officials decide the value of particular jobs. In the United States, that role belongs to the marketplace.

So what should be done instead?

To improve transparency, every part of a CEO’s pay and benefits should be disclosed regularly and completely. That means planes, automobiles, golf-club memberships, bonuses, stock options, retirement arrangements and salaries — essentially anything a reasonable person would view as part of a chief executive’s compensation package. See Fiorina discuss executive pay, including her own.

To increase accountability, shareholders should vote each year on every element of CEO compensation. In the end, the people who own a company should decide whether a chief executive’s rewards are warranted by that executive’s performance. Since American taxpayers now hold partial ownership stakes in many companies, the government should also have a vote — in some instances, a very large one.

Additionally, “clawback provisions” should become routine. These rules would require a CEO to give compensation back to shareholders if promised results are not achieved.

Finally, when a corporation asks Washington for taxpayer funds, it is effectively acknowledging that serious errors were made and that important risks did not pay off. In those circumstances, CEOs should be ready to submit their resignations, along with the resignations of their boards. Receiving a bailout should require accountability from both the chief executive and the board.

We must avoid damaging the economy in the process of trying to repair it. These are hard times. President Obama has called the current moment a “crisis” and warned of a looming “catastrophe.” In moments like these, action is necessary. But the important thing is to choose measures that provide short-term help while also making sense over the medium and long term.

Too often, political leaders respond to emergencies and public outrage by going too far, creating unexpected problems that only become obvious later. In America, the chance to earn rewards for taking responsible risks is central to our economic energy and strength. Anger over Wall Street greed and excess should not cause us to abandon that essential principle.

The views expressed in this commentary belong solely to Carly Fiorina.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style opinion commentary by Carly Fiorina about President Obama’s proposed $500,000 executive pay cap for bailed-out Wall Street firms, arguing that CEO pay outrage is justified but government should not set salaries.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Carly Fiorina’s exact voice or style, but here is an original CNN-style opinion commentary that reflects the kind of business-and-government argument a former CEO and political figure might make.

---

## Outrage over CEO pay is justified. A government salary cap is still the wrong answer.

The anger is real, and it is understandable.

At a time when millions of Americans are losing jobs, watching retirement savings shrink and wondering whether their homes and small businesses will survive, it is infuriating to see executives at bailed-out Wall Street firms collect enormous compensation packages. Many of these institutions made reckless decisions, took excessive risks and then turned to taxpayers for rescue when those risks collapsed.

So let’s be clear: outrage over executive pay is not class warfare. It is common sense.

When a company fails badly enough that it needs government support to stay alive, its leaders have lost the moral authority to behave as though nothing has changed. Bonuses for failure offend basic notions of fairness. Rewards should follow results, not political access or taxpayer protection.

But President Obama’s proposal to cap executive pay at $500,000 for companies receiving extraordinary bailout assistance raises a serious question: Should the federal government set salaries in private enterprise?

The answer should be no.

Government has every right — indeed, an obligation — to attach conditions to taxpayer money. If a firm accepts public rescue funds, taxpayers deserve transparency, accountability and strict limits on abuse. Boards should be required to justify compensation. Bonuses should be tied to long-term performance, not short-term gambling. Executives should not be rewarded for driving their companies into the ditch and then handing the repair bill to the public.

But there is a difference between demanding accountability and having Washington decide what a chief executive, trader, engineer or manager is allowed to earn.

Once government begins setting compensation levels, even in unpopular industries, the precedent is dangerous. Today it is Wall Street executives. Tomorrow it may be health care, energy, manufacturing, technology or any other sector that finds itself dependent on federal contracts, subsidies, loans or regulation. In a modern economy, the boundary between government involvement and private enterprise is already blurry enough.

The problem on Wall Street was not merely that some people were paid too much. It was that they were paid in the wrong way.

Compensation systems rewarded short-term gains while ignoring long-term risk. Executives and traders could benefit from transactions that looked profitable in one quarter but proved disastrous later. Boards failed to exercise proper oversight. Shareholders were often too passive. Regulators missed warning signs. And when the consequences arrived, taxpayers were asked to step in.

A flat salary cap does not fix those structural failures.

In fact, it may create new problems. Talented people needed to unwind complex assets, restructure failing institutions and return taxpayer money may leave for firms not subject to the cap. That does not mean every executive deserves sympathy. Many do not. But taxpayers should want these companies repaired, stabilized and removed from government support as quickly as possible. Symbolic punishment is not the same as effective reform.

A better approach would focus on three principles.

First, no rewards for failure. Companies receiving extraordinary taxpayer assistance should not pay large bonuses to executives whose decisions contributed to collapse. Compensation should be tied to measurable recovery, repayment of public funds and long-term financial health.

Second, full transparency. If taxpayers are effectively investors, they deserve to know how executives are being paid and why. Compensation packages should be disclosed clearly, not hidden in complex benefits, deferred arrangements or perks.

Third, real board accountability. Boards of directors, not politicians, should set pay — but boards must do their jobs. If they approve excessive compensation at taxpayer-supported firms, they should be held responsible by shareholders, regulators and, where appropriate, Congress through oversight.

The public is right to demand that Wall Street learn humility. The executives who helped create this crisis should not be insulated from its consequences. Capitalism depends on accountability. When people are rewarded for success, they must also bear consequences for failure.

But capitalism also depends on limits to government power. We should be careful not to let justified anger produce policies that expand Washington’s role in ways we may later regret.

The goal should not be to have politicians decide what every executive is worth. The goal should be to ensure that no executive can privatize the gains, socialize the losses and then expect taxpayers to applaud.

Wall Street needs reform. Taxpayers deserve protection. Executive pay must be tied to performance and responsibility.

But government should not become America’s compensation committee.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an op-ed from the perspective of former HP CEO Carly Fiorina responding to public anger over Wall Street compensation after the financial bailout, emphasizing transparency, shareholder votes, clawbacks, and CEO accountability instead of federal pay caps.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Better Answer to Wall Street Pay: Accountability, Not Washington Pay Caps**  
*By Carly Fiorina*

Americans are right to be angry.

After taxpayers were asked to rescue major financial institutions from collapse, many families watched Wall Street return quickly to business as usual: large bonuses, complex compensation packages, and too little evidence that the lessons of the crisis had been learned. Millions of Americans lost jobs, homes, savings, or confidence in the system. They deserve more than explanations. They deserve accountability.

But anger, however justified, does not always produce the right policy. The question before us is not whether compensation on Wall Street should change. It must. The question is who should set it, how it should be set, and how we ensure that executives are rewarded for building lasting value rather than taking short-term risks with other people’s money.

Federal pay caps may sound satisfying, but they are the wrong tool. They invite political management of private enterprise, encourage loopholes, and risk turning compensation into another Washington bargaining exercise. Worse, they do not address the real problem: too many boards and executives created pay systems disconnected from performance, risk, and long-term shareholder value.

The better answer is transparency, shareholder power, clawbacks, and real CEO accountability.

First, compensation must be clear enough for owners to understand. Shareholders cannot hold boards accountable if pay packages are buried in jargon, hidden in deferred arrangements, or obscured by formulas few people can decipher. Every company should disclose plainly how much senior executives are paid, what performance metrics determine that pay, what risks are being rewarded, and how compensation aligns with long-term results.

Second, shareholders should have a meaningful vote on executive compensation. A “say on pay” vote gives owners a direct voice and forces boards to defend their decisions. It does not put politicians in charge of pay, and it does not substitute public outrage for business judgment. It strengthens the basic principle of capitalism: owners have rights, and management works for them.

Third, compensation should be subject to clawbacks. If executives are paid bonuses based on results that later prove false, inflated, or dependent on excessive risk-taking, they should not keep the money. Rewards earned on paper but destroyed in reality are not rewards; they are mistakes. A serious clawback policy would make clear that executives cannot cash out before the consequences of their decisions are known.

Fourth, CEOs must be accountable for the cultures they create. No chief executive can personally approve every trade or every loan. But the CEO is responsible for incentives, values, risk controls, and the people placed in positions of authority. If a company rewards volume without regard to quality, leverage without regard to prudence, or short-term gain without regard to long-term health, that is a leadership failure.

Accountability should begin in the boardroom. Boards of directors have a duty to represent shareholders, not to rubber-stamp management’s wishes. Compensation committees must be independent, informed, and willing to say no. They should design pay that rewards sustainable performance, penalizes failure, and recognizes that leadership is about stewardship as well as success.

None of this means we should punish success. America’s economic strength has always depended on risk-taking, innovation, and the opportunity to be rewarded for exceptional performance. We should not create a system in which Washington decides what a talented manager, entrepreneur, or executive may earn. That path leads to politicized decision-making and weaker companies.

But defending the free market does not mean defending every practice that occurs in it. Capitalism depends on trust. It depends on the belief that rewards are earned, risks are borne by those who take them, and failure has consequences. When gains are privatized and losses are socialized, public trust is shattered.

The financial bailout created a special obligation. Institutions that accepted taxpayer assistance cannot pretend nothing changed. They owe taxpayers transparency. They owe shareholders honesty. They owe employees and customers better leadership. And they owe the country proof that compensation systems will no longer encourage reckless behavior at public expense.

Washington should set clear rules for disclosure, shareholder rights, and recovery of unearned compensation. It should not set salaries. The goal should be to restore accountability, not replace boards of directors with members of Congress.

The American people are not wrong to demand change. They are right. But the change we need is not symbolic punishment. It is structural reform that makes executives answerable to owners, boards answerable to shareholders, and pay answerable to performance.

That is how we rebuild trust. That is how we strengthen capitalism. And that is how we ensure that when executives succeed, they do so by creating real and lasting value—not by taking risks that someone else is forced to pay for.

**Editor’s Note:** Carly Fiorina is the former chair and chief executive officer of Hewlett-Packard, a former Republican presidential candidate, and a longtime commentator on business, leadership, and public policy.

# Executive Pay Caps Are Understandable — but They Won’t Fix Banking

Public anger over executive compensation at taxpayer-supported banks is not only understandable; it is justified. When financial institutions require extraordinary public assistance to survive, executives should not expect to conduct business as usual. Taxpayers who helped stabilize the banking system have every right to ask why leaders whose firms needed rescue should continue receiving lavish pay packages, bonuses, and perks.

But understandable anger does not always produce effective policy. Limiting executive compensation at banks that receive taxpayer support may satisfy a legitimate desire for accountability, yet it risks treating a symptom rather than the disease. The deeper problem is not merely that some executives were paid too much. It is that the financial system rewarded short-term risk-taking while insulating key decision-makers from the long-term consequences of failure.

That is a governance problem, a market discipline problem, and a regulatory design problem. Pay caps alone cannot solve it.

## Why the Pay Cap Argument Resonates

The case for limiting compensation is simple: if a bank depends on public money, then taxpayers become unwilling investors. No private company has an inherent right to unlimited compensation when its survival is being underwritten by citizens.

In ordinary circumstances, executive pay should be set by boards, shareholders, and the market for talent. But taxpayer-supported banks are not operating under ordinary circumstances. They benefit from emergency capital, guarantees, liquidity support, or implicit protection from failure. In that environment, outrage over multi-million-dollar bonuses is not populism; it is a reaction to moral hazard.

When profits are privatized and losses are socialized, the public naturally demands conditions. Compensation limits are one way to signal that public support comes with obligations.

## Why Compensation Caps Are Flawed

Still, broad government-imposed pay limits carry serious risks.

First, they can drive talent away from troubled institutions precisely when competent management is needed most. A failing bank does not become healthier because its leadership is cheaper. It becomes healthier when management is capable of restructuring balance sheets, restoring confidence, raising private capital, and making disciplined lending decisions.

Second, pay caps often encourage evasive behavior. Companies can shift compensation into deferred benefits, consulting contracts, retention awards, stock grants, or other forms that may be less transparent. The result can be more complexity rather than more accountability.

Third, government pay-setting can become political. Once Washington begins determining what executives “should” earn, compensation decisions may be influenced by headlines, election cycles, and public anger rather than performance, risk, and long-term value creation.

Most importantly, compensation limits do not necessarily change incentives. A capped salary can still reward bad judgment if it is not tied to risk-adjusted long-term performance. Conversely, a large pay package can be defensible if it is earned over time, subject to clawbacks, and linked to durable results.

The issue is not simply how much executives are paid. It is what they are paid for.

## The Real Problem: Incentives Without Consequences

The financial crisis revealed that too many institutions rewarded volume over quality, leverage over resilience, and short-term gains over long-term stability. Executives and traders could be compensated for profits that later evaporated. Boards often failed to challenge management. Shareholders lacked sufficient power or information. Creditors assumed large institutions would be rescued rather than allowed to fail.

In that environment, compensation caps are a blunt instrument. They may punish visible executives, but they do not restore market discipline.

A better system would ensure that those who make decisions bear consequences when those decisions go wrong. That requires reforms that use markets, ownership, transparency, and accountability rather than political micromanagement.

## Market-Based Reforms That Would Work Better

### 1. Require More Compensation to Be Deferred

Executives at taxpayer-supported banks should not receive large immediate rewards for gains that may disappear in future years. A significant portion of compensation should be deferred and paid out over time, based on the long-term performance of the institution.

This does not require Washington to decide a CEO’s salary. It requires boards to structure pay so that rewards are earned only if results prove durable.

### 2. Expand Clawbacks for Failure and Misconduct

If profits were based on excessive risk, accounting errors, regulatory violations, or losses that emerge later, bonuses should be recoverable. Clawback provisions should apply not only in cases of fraud but also when performance metrics were materially misleading.

This would align incentives more effectively than arbitrary caps. Executives would know that short-term gains cannot be cashed out permanently if long-term damage follows.

### 3. Pay Executives in Long-Term Equity

Executives should hold meaningful equity that vests over several years and cannot be quickly sold. The goal is to make leaders think like long-term owners, not short-term bonus recipients.

At banks receiving taxpayer support, equity-based compensation should be especially tied to repayment of public funds, capital strength, loan performance, and sustainable profitability.

### 4. Strengthen Shareholder Oversight

Shareholders should have a stronger voice in approving executive compensation plans. “Say on pay” votes, greater disclosure, and more independent compensation committees can help restore accountability.

Boards should be required to explain clearly how compensation reflects risk, performance, and long-term value. If shareholders dislike the plan, they should be able to apply pressure without waiting for a crisis.

### 5. Make Bank Failure Credible

The most powerful market discipline is the possibility of failure. If creditors, boards, and executives believe a large bank will always be rescued, they will take more risk than they should.

Policymakers need credible resolution mechanisms that allow large financial institutions to fail without bringing down the system. That means living wills, stronger capital requirements, orderly liquidation authority, and rules that impose losses on shareholders and unsecured creditors before taxpayers are exposed.

Compensation reform matters, but it cannot substitute for ending “too big to fail.”

### 6. Increase Capital Requirements and Risk Transparency

Banks that hold more capital are less likely to need bailouts. Higher capital standards, especially for systemically important institutions, reduce the subsidy created by implicit government backing.

Markets also need better information. Investors should be able to understand a bank’s leverage, asset quality, off-balance-sheet exposure, and risk concentration. Transparency allows markets to price risk more accurately and punish reckless institutions before taxpayers are asked to intervene.

### 7. Price Taxpayer Support Like a Market Transaction

If government support is provided, it should not be treated as a political favor or a blank check. Taxpayers should receive warrants, preferred shares, fees, or other compensation that reflects the risk being assumed.

The goal should be to make public assistance expensive enough that private capital is preferred whenever possible. Government aid should stabilize the system, not subsidize failure.

## Accountability Without Political Control

The challenge is to balance two principles. Taxpayers deserve protection when public money is used. But private enterprise cannot function well if political officials routinely dictate compensation, strategy, and management decisions.

That is why the better approach is not permanent government control over executive pay. It is to redesign incentives so that executives, boards, shareholders, and creditors face the consequences of their decisions.

Compensation should be transparent. Rewards should be tied to long-term performance. Bonuses should be subject to clawback. Shareholders should have real oversight. Creditors should not assume automatic rescue. Banks should hold enough capital to absorb losses. And when public support is necessary, taxpayers should be compensated for the risk.

Executive pay caps may answer public anger, but they will not rebuild a healthy banking system. Accountability requires more than limiting salaries. It requires restoring market discipline — the essential force that rewards success, punishes failure, and protects taxpayers from being forced to rescue the same mistakes again.

**Commentary: Capitalism Needs Accountability, Not Political Pay-Setting**

*February 2009*

The anger in America today is real, and it is justified.

Millions of Americans are worried about their jobs, their homes, their retirement savings and their children’s futures. They have watched venerable financial institutions fail or survive only because taxpayers stepped in. They have seen executives receive bonuses even as their companies lost billions, laid off workers or required extraordinary government assistance.

When citizens are asked to shoulder the cost of rescuing private companies, they have every right to demand accountability.

But as Washington debates President Obama’s proposal to cap compensation for executives at firms receiving substantial taxpayer bailout funds, we should be careful not to confuse two very different questions. The first is whether executives whose companies depend on taxpayer money should be held to rigorous standards. They should. The second is whether government should become the permanent arbiter of private-sector pay. It should not.

Capitalism is not a system in which success is guaranteed or failure is subsidized indefinitely. It is a system built on risk, reward, competition, innovation and accountability. When it works properly, those who create value are rewarded, and those who fail bear the consequences.

In recent years, however, too many boards and executives lost sight of that basic principle. Compensation packages in some companies became disconnected from long-term performance. Rewards were paid for short-term gains, even when those gains were created by excessive leverage, poor risk management or accounting illusions. Too often, executives benefited when times were good, while employees, shareholders and ultimately taxpayers paid the price when things went bad.

That is not capitalism. That is a failure of accountability.

President Obama’s instinct to respond to public outrage is understandable. If a company cannot survive without taxpayer support, then taxpayers are no longer merely observers; they are stakeholders. It is reasonable to impose conditions on extraordinary assistance. No executive at a company living on public funds should expect business as usual.

Limits on cash compensation, restrictions on golden parachutes, clawbacks for bonuses based on false results and stronger disclosure requirements are all legitimate tools when taxpayer money is at risk. The public deserves to know that rescue funds are being used to stabilize the economy, preserve jobs and restore lending — not to insulate executives from the consequences of their own decisions.

But we must also recognize the danger of governing by outrage. Compensation caps may satisfy a political need in the short term, but they are a blunt instrument. Poorly designed, they can drive talent away from precisely the institutions we need to repair. They can encourage companies to find loopholes. They can substitute Washington’s judgment for the judgment of shareholders, boards and markets.

The goal should not be to punish success. Nor should it be to make government a permanent compensation committee for American enterprise. The goal should be to restore responsibility.

That begins with boards of directors. Boards must do their jobs. They must ensure that pay is tied to sustainable, long-term performance — not quarterly engineering or reckless risk-taking. They must be independent, informed and willing to say no. Compensation committees should ask hard questions: Are incentives aligned with shareholder value? Are risks properly measured? Are rewards earned over time? Can bonuses be recovered if results prove illusory?

Shareholders also deserve a stronger voice. Owners of companies should have better tools to hold boards accountable for compensation decisions. Transparency matters. Sunlight matters. If a pay package cannot be explained clearly to shareholders, employees and the public, perhaps it cannot be justified.

Executives, too, must remember that leadership is not entitlement. Leadership means accepting responsibility. In difficult times, it means sharing sacrifice. The best leaders understand that credibility is earned not only through results, but through judgment, restraint and integrity.

At the same time, we should resist the temptation to demonize all CEOs or all business leaders. America’s prosperity has been built by entrepreneurs, innovators, investors, managers and workers who take risks and build enterprises. Most businesses are not asking for bailouts. Most executives are trying to keep people employed, serve customers and navigate a severe recession.

We need successful companies. We need profits. We need investment. We need people willing to take risks and create jobs. If we turn legitimate anger into hostility toward capitalism itself, we will damage the very engine that must power our recovery.

The financial crisis has revealed serious failures: failures of regulation, failures of risk management, failures of corporate governance and failures of leadership. Government has a role to play in correcting those failures. But government cannot replace the market, and it cannot manage every business decision from Washington.

The right answer is neither unchecked executive privilege nor permanent government control. The right answer is accountable capitalism.

Companies that take taxpayer money must accept taxpayer conditions. Executives who destroy value should not be rewarded as though they created it. Boards must be held responsible for the incentives they approve. Shareholders must have greater transparency and influence. Regulators must focus on systemic risk without smothering innovation.

Americans do not begrudge success when it is earned. What they reject is reward without responsibility.

If we remember that distinction, we can reform executive compensation without undermining capitalism. We can protect taxpayers without turning Washington into the nation’s paymaster. And we can emerge from this crisis with a stronger, more responsible free enterprise system — one worthy of the confidence of the American people.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an opinion column arguing that Wall Street executives receiving bailout money should disclose all perks and compensation, face shareholder approval and clawbacks, and possibly resign, but should not have their salaries arbitrarily capped by the government.
counterfactuals.output:
**Don’t Cap Wall Street Pay. Expose It, Vote on It, and Claw It Back.**

There is something deeply galling about watching Wall Street executives, whose firms survived only because taxpayers stepped in, continue to enjoy private jets, lavish perks and enormous compensation packages as if nothing happened. When a company takes bailout money, it is no longer just another private enterprise making private decisions. It has accepted public rescue, and with that rescue should come public accountability.

But accountability is not the same thing as Washington arbitrarily setting salaries.

The government should not be in the business of deciding that a bank executive may earn exactly $500,000, $1 million or any other politically convenient number. Such caps may satisfy public anger, but they are a blunt instrument. They risk turning compensation policy into a theatrical contest in which lawmakers compete to look tough while doing little to fix the incentives that helped create the crisis in the first place.

The real problem was not simply that executives were paid too much. It was that they were paid too much for taking risks whose costs they did not personally bear. They could collect bonuses when bets paid off and leave shareholders, workers and taxpayers holding the bag when those bets collapsed. That is the system that must be changed.

The first requirement should be full disclosure. Any company receiving bailout funds should be required to disclose, in plain language, every significant form of executive compensation: salary, bonuses, stock grants, options, pensions, deferred compensation, severance agreements, personal use of corporate aircraft, housing allowances, club memberships, security arrangements and any other perks that effectively transfer corporate wealth to top managers.

No more hiding compensation in footnotes. No more labeling luxuries as necessities. If taxpayers are helping keep a firm alive, taxpayers deserve to know how the firm is rewarding its leaders.

Second, compensation packages at bailed-out firms should be subject to meaningful shareholder approval. Shareholders are the owners of the company, and they should have a direct voice in whether executives who presided over catastrophic losses deserve bonuses, retention awards or golden parachutes. In the case of institutions propped up by public money, the government, as a major financial backer, should use its leverage to demand stronger governance rather than merely impose symbolic pay ceilings.

Third, there must be clawbacks. If executives receive bonuses based on profits that later prove illusory, fraudulent or dependent on excessive risk, the company should be able to recover that money. Compensation should be tied to long-term performance, not quarterly mirages. A bonus earned by loading a balance sheet with hidden dangers is not a reward for success; it is an advance payment on failure.

Clawbacks should apply not only in cases of outright fraud but also where compensation was based on misstated earnings, concealed losses or strategies that produced short-term gains while inflicting long-term damage. Executives who demand the upside of capitalism must accept its downside too.

And yes, in some cases, executives should resign.

If a chief executive led a firm into ruin and then turned to taxpayers for rescue, it is fair to ask whether that person has forfeited the moral and managerial authority to remain in charge. Resignation should not be automatic in every case; some institutions may need continuity, and some managers may be better suited than replacements to unwind the damage. But bailout money should not become a shield protecting failed leaders from consequences. Boards should be expected to justify publicly why top executives remain in place.

What should be avoided, however, is the seductive simplicity of government salary caps. Once politicians begin setting pay by decree, compensation decisions become less about performance and more about optics. Firms may respond by finding loopholes, shifting pay into benefits, delaying compensation or losing capable employees to institutions not subject to the same restrictions. Worse, salary caps can distract from the harder and more important task of reforming incentives.

The goal should not be to make every Wall Street executive poorer by government order. The goal should be to make executives responsible.

A compensation system built on transparency, shareholder control and clawbacks is harder to game and more consistent with a market economy. It says: If you want to be paid like a capitalist, act like one. Put your rewards at risk. Let the owners approve them. Give the money back if the results were phony. And if you failed badly enough to require a taxpayer rescue, be prepared to give up your office along with your bonus.

Public outrage over bailout pay is justified. Taxpayers did not rescue Wall Street so executives could preserve every privilege of failure. But anger should produce reform, not political wage-setting.

Wall Street does not need arbitrary salary caps. It needs sunlight, accountability and consequences.
